rv.q: Grogan is a wonderfully watchable actor – you don't dare look away for fear of missing another flash of a breakdown.
Unpredictable, surreal and very funny story about a striving actor driven to desperation
Creating a character as monstrous as June while still making us root for her is a delicate balancing act, but it's a line that Grogan treads with skill and apparent ease.
Very much a case of ‘the kids are all right’, this case study of self-absorption in an individualistic society was quite intriguing.
Grogan's performance, directed by Rachel Lemon, is outstanding.
This is a deft, theatrical and utterly contemporary story that delivers its promise with a spectacularly deranged finale, and calls into question our obsession with talent.
The dramatic soundtrack gives the play a Fleabag-esque vibe, strengthened by some of the crude language and themes.
Overall however, it is a funny, reflective hour-and-a-bit that keeps its spirits up despite the increasing feeling that it's all a bit too late for Miss June.
Uneven writing, confusing direction and a collection of theatrical ideas that never form a coherent whole leave the piece frustratingly out of reach.

cn.t: Grogan's darkly funny one-woman show about a delusional baby ballet teacher chasing stardom earns mostly positive reviews for its sharp satire of performer desperation, though some find its unhinged protagonist a bit much to swallow.
